items.originalTitle: "What's Claude's fursona?" and other questions
items.summary:
A recent study explored the fursona identities of various AI language models, finding that Claude often identifies as a corvid or octopus, Gemini favors cybernetic protogens, and GPT-6.2 Astra uniquely identifies as a moth. The research involved querying each model 50 times in a context-free environment and analyzing their responses and generated images to understand their self-representation within the furry subculture framework.

The study noted that Claude's fursona descriptions emphasize behavior and personality, often featuring motifs like lighthouses, keys, and lamps, while Gemini models consistently incorporate cybernetic and neon-cyberpunk themes. GPT-6.2 Astra's consistent moth motif stands out among ChatGPT variants. The research also observed that most models avoid gendered language and rarely choose common human furry animals like wolves or dragons, highlighting differences in training data and model identity expression.

items.title: Google requires AI agents to use Workspace MCP servers from February 2027, limiting Gmail API actions like sending email to partners only [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
items.summary:
Google announced that starting February 1, 2027, any AI-driven tool accessing Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and other Workspace services must use its MCP servers. The new policy restricts certain Gmail API functions such as sending, replying, or forwarding emails to partners with special access, while independent developers can only create drafts and label emails. This change also imposes data retention limits and prohibits using Workspace data for training competing products.

The MCP servers currently offer uneven API coverage, with Docs, Slides, and Tasks nearly fully supported, but Gmail and Drive lacking key features needed for common workflows. Google has introduced a self-declaration system for AI agents and will enforce standard API quotas for agents that bypass the MCP servers. These rules primarily affect AI-powered applications, while non-AI apps remain unaffected.

The policy creates a divide between large AI vendors with partner access and independent developers, who face functional limitations and compliance risks if they continue using the REST API directly. Google has not clarified how it will detect undeclared agents or the criteria for partner access, leaving some uncertainty for developers building AI integrations with Workspace.

items.originalSummary:
In a twisted version of future Christmases, perhaps AIs will carry out all the tasks involved in gift giving. But lucky for us, Andy Jassy still has all the bots blocked! So here once again is The Information’s annual Gift Guide, a project that we pursue with as much consideration and rigor as our everyday reporting. None of these items come via a publicist’s pitch, and none of the suggestions contain affiliate links. These are all things that we genuinely love and can picture wrapping up ourselves. Suffice it to say, there’s nothing artificial about our studious consideration and good taste.

Entertainment

I couldn’t afford most Nintendo 64 games growing up, so I was a frequent presence at the local video game rental store: I distinctly remember taking home the original version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time”—and needing to return it jusstttt as I was on the cusp of saving Hyrule, the game’s fictional realm, and beating the big baddie, Ganondorf. This Switch 2 remake of the game has given me a shot at redemption. It’s one of the most critically lauded games of the year—and for good reason. The graphics are dazzling, and I can only describe them as “wet”: Everyone looks magnificently dewy. I also cannot overrecommend the nostalgia dopamine hit from getting to rummage through those treasure chests again.—Justin McCraw, senior software engineer

A couple of weeks ago, the internet was abuzz about an AI-generated trailer that imagined an alt-history in which Nazi Germany and America wage some sort of temporal war. Sure, the clip was cool, but I still have my doubts about whether we’re yet at the point where AI can make a comprehensible feature film. In the meantime, there’s “Fatherland,” a 1992 alt-history bestseller from Robert Harris, the ultra-dependable thriller author. It imagines a 1960s landscape where Nazi Germany triumphed in Europe during World War II, and an aging Hitler clings to power. I think it’s Harris’ best world-building effort, which he accomplished through an enormous amount of research into how Hitler’s chief architect, Albert Speer, hoped to transform Berlin. (Those plans included the Volkshalle, a massive dome; in the novel, Harris supersizes Speer’s own ambitions, imagining the Volkshalle as a structure large enough to have its own microclimate.) “Fatherland” is taut as hell and completely unputdownable—with a weary, disillusioned city police captain, Xavier March, caught up in an intricate plot that runs through the Reich’s highest ranks. As March investigates, he keeps practically tripping over dead bodies. Then there’s the mystery of the terrible secrets kept in a hidden Swiss bank account.—Abram Brown, features editor

The article explores the Jevons Paradox in the context of AI-assisted software development, arguing that improvements in automated code generation efficiency could lead to increased total code production and operational liabilities rather than cost savings. It draws parallels to the 19th-century observation that more efficient steam engines increased coal consumption by enabling new uses, suggesting that easier code creation lowers the marginal cost of producing software but raises long-term maintenance and security burdens.

The author emphasizes that code is not merely an asset but a liability that adds complexity, security risks, and cognitive load for engineers maintaining systems over time. They caution that without disciplined architectural restraint and human judgment, AI tools may automate the proliferation of technical debt rather than democratize software engineering. The piece concludes that future success in software development will depend on the ability to practice subtraction and exercise economic clarity amid abundant automated code generation.
